title: Scheduler pipeline latency (p95) fanout - post-incident notes
content:
Summary:

On 2024-11-03 between 04:12 - 05:05 UTC we observed a sustained spike in kube-scheduler p95 scheduling latency (from baseline ~30ms to >3.2s) and a corresponding increase in podPending counts across several clusters in prod-us-west-2. Customer-facing impact: short bursts of request queueing for new model load jobs and longer pod start times for autoscaling jobs. No data loss, no control-plane outage, but higher tail latency for user jobs and multiple automated retries causing transactional fanout.

Short timeline (rough):
- 04:12 UTC: Alert: scheduler.p95 > 2s for >1m (alerting rule: SRE-SCHED-LAT-01).
- 04:14 UTC: Pager duty engagement. Initial slack thread started #sre-incident-2024-11-03.
- 04:16 UTC: Noticed etcd leader churn on control plane host cp-3 (etcd leader changes at ~04:10-04:15).
- 04:20 UTC: CNI pod restarts observed on a subset of nodes (cilium-agent restart loop) correlating with kernel upgrades happening on a fraction of spot nodes earlier that morning.
- 04:27 UTC: kube-apiserver request latencies elevated; kube-scheduler log shows `(ListAndWatch) watch closed` errors and backlog.
- 04:35 UTC: Temporary mitigation: scaled scheduler replicas from 2 -> 4 for clusters with control-plane HA enabled (helped coordination).
- 04:45 UTC: Applied k8s-apiserver-sidepatch to reduce watchList memory by enabling watch compression and small client timeout tweaks (rolled to cp-1/2/3).
- 05:05 UTC: p95 stabilized near baseline, podPending dropped, tickets opened for follow-ups.

Primary observations and evidence: 
- Metrics: Prometheus series kube_scheduler_schedule_duration_seconds_bucket showed p95 jumping from 0.03 -> 3.2. kube_apiserver_request_duration_seconds had matching tail latency increases on GET/watch endpoints.
- Logs: scheduler logs contained repeated `failed to list *v1.Pod: etcdserver: request timed out` entries.
- Etcd: etcd stats showed increased leader election rate and compaction backlog; disk-io wait on cp-3 (iostat showed iowait spikes).
- CNI: cilium agent logs on affected nodes show intermittent `Conntrack table transient overflow` warnings followed by agent restarts; kernel dmesg contained OOM_killer events on a few worker nodes earlier that morning.
- Workloads: Large fanout job (model-snapshot-rollout) opened ~1200 small pods over a 40s window which amplified the control-plane load.

Root cause hypothesis (contributing factors):
1) Control-plane IO contention: cp-3 had underlying noisy neighbor disk I/O resulting in delayed etcd responses and leader elections. Etcd leader churn caused transient inconsistencies for list/watch queries used by scheduler and controllers.
2) High fanout of short-lived pods: our large rollout test opened many pods with tight creation windows. Scheduler experienced a work-queue backlog and apiserver watch pressure.
3) CNI instability on spot nodes: kernel upgrades + memory pressure on a subset of edge nodes triggered cilium restarts and conntrack churn, increasing API churn as node status updates and pod status updates spiked.
4) Scheduler tuning headroom: scheduler replicas and client QPS/burst settings at kube-apiserver were insufficient to absorb this combined control-plane spike.

Mitigations applied during incident (ordered):
- Increased kube-scheduler replicas (2 -> 4) on affected clusters to widen scheduling throughput immediately.
- Disabled the problematic rollout job (paused the model-snapshot-run) and rate-limited subsequent rollout jobs with a temporary admission webhook rule (manual block).
- Rebooted cp-3 after cordoning non-critical control-plane processes to recover from disk noisy neighbor (coordinated with infra team).
- Applied temporary API server tweak: reduced watchtimeout to 30s and enabled response compression for watch streams to reduce memory pressure on apiserver (rolled to canary cp-1 then to others).
- Drained and reprovisioned 12 spot nodes that had kernel upgrade anomalies; reintroduced with validated kernel version and cilium edge agent pinned.

What didn’t help / dead ends: 
- Temporarily increasing etcd timeouts without addressing disk IO did not reduce leader churn.
- Trying to bump kube-apiserver CPU limits mid-incident had minimal effect until we reduced incoming watch/list fanout.

Immediate follow-ups and actions (owner and ETA):
- [Diego Alvarez] - Run a full disk IO health sweep across control-plane hosts and schedule maintenance window to migrate etcd leader off cp-3 if needed (ETA 2024-11-10).
- [Priya Nair] - Add rate-limit admission controller for high-fanout controllers (config: per-namespace concurrent pod creation cap). Prototype by 2024-11-17, rollout after testing.
- [Samir Gupta] - Implement an automated spot-node kernel validation job that prevents 1-click kernel upgrades without passing cilium smoke tests (ETA 2024-11-20).
- [Maya Henderson] - Proposal: increase kube-scheduler to 3 replicas by default for all prod clusters and tune QPS/burst settings in apiserver for scheduler client. PR by 2024-11-14.
- [Infra] - Evaluate moving etcd data volume to higher iops tier for cp-3 class instances or add io-throttling protections for neighbor disks (investigate by 2024-11-12).

Runbook draft additions (quick mitigation playbook):
- Trigger when scheduler.p95 > 1s for >2m AND pending_pods_by_cluster > 50: 
  1) Pause any ongoing high-fanout jobs via admission webhook or disable CI triggers.
  2) Check etcd leader info: `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table` and `etcdctl endpoint health` for latency.
  3) If leader churn observed, check disk iowait on control-plane nodes: `ssh cp-N sudo iostat -x 1 5` and open infra ticket.
  4) Temporarily scale kube-scheduler replicas (kubectl scale deployment/kube-scheduler -n kube-system --replicas=4).
  5) If CNI restarts detected (cilium/cni logs): cordon affected nodes and drain non-critical pods, reprovision nodes.
  6) If immediate recovery not achieved, enable apiserver watch compression and reduce watch timeout to 20-30s; roll to canary control-plane first.
  7) Post-incident, run pod creation rate audit to identify noisy controllers.

Open questions / uncertainties: 
- How much of the scheduler backlog was solely due to apiserver watch pressure vs scheduler CPU? We need a tighter correlation analysis (trace individual scheduling latencies per pod).
- Would preemptively increasing scheduler replicas (and default apiserver burst) increase overall stability or mask a deeper etctd IO problem?
- Are there controller patterns in our deployments that produce pathological pod create/delete churn (e.g., aggressive liveness probes + rapid restarts) that we can throttle?

Suggested metrics to add for future detection: 
- Per-namespace pod creation rate (5s granularity) and alert on >200 creations over 1m for single namespace.
- Etcd request latency percentiles with per-endpoint breakdown and iowait correlation tags.
- Cilium conntrack overflow rate and agent restart counts as an early alert.

Notes / artifacts clipped here: 
- Example scheduler error snippet: `E1103 04:16:23.512345 1 factory.go:125] error listing Pods: etcdserver: request timed out`
- Etcd endpoint peek: `endpoint: https://10.0.0.5:2379, status: healthy, latency: 1.7s` (during spike)
- Sample prom query used: `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kube_scheduler_schedule_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))`

Retrospective notes (tone):
- This incident was H -> M severity: it revealed an important interplay between spot node stability (CNI), cluster-scale fanout jobs, and control-plane IO. There was no single catastrophic bug — instead a multiplicative effect: noisy neighbor IO + many small pods + CNI churn drove apiserver and etcd into tail latency which cascaded to scheduler backlog.
- The immediate mitigations were effective: pausing the fanout and scaling scheduler replicas bought time; but long-term fixes must reduce the likelihood of the same multi-factor alignment.

End of notes.

Appendix: quick commands used during triage (copyable):
- kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200
- kubectl top nodes
- etcdctl --endpoints=https://cp-3:2379 endpoint status --write-out=table
- journalctl -u kube-apiserver -f --since 2024-11-03
